summary.text: Gas is a state of matter with neither fixed volume nor fixed shape, and it is a compressible form of fluid, unlike a liquid.
What sets gases apart from liquids and solids is the vast separation of their particles, which can make some gases invisible.
Gases are described by four properties: pressure, volume, number of particles and temperature, and studying them led to the ideal gas law.

facts.value: Pressure, volume, number of particles and temperature

facts.value: Used first by chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont, early 17th century

items.prompt: Why can you walk through a room full of some gases without seeing anything?

options.label: The particles are too heavy to reflect any light
The particles move too quickly to be seen at all
The particles are so far apart that some gases are invisible
The particles are packed so tightly they blend into the air

items.explain: The vast separation of gas particles can make some gases invisible to a human observer.

items.prompt: You push the plunger of a sealed syringe full of gas. What do you expect to happen to the gas?

options.label: It squeezes into less room, which a liquid would not do
It stays exactly the same size, like a liquid
It leaks out through the sides of the syringe
It turns into a solid under the force

items.explain: A gas is a compressible form of fluid, in contrast to a liquid.

items.prompt: In a J-shaped tube, a trapped gas with fixed temperature and particle count is pushed on by more mercury. What does the gas do?

options.label: It takes up more space
It stays the same size
It warms up and expands
It takes up less space

items.explain: Boyle added mercury to raise the pressure and saw the trapped gas's volume decrease, an inverse relationship.

items.prompt: A chemist wants to describe a sample of gas fully. Which set of measurements does she need?

options.label: Pressure, volume, density and viscosity
Pressure, volume, number of particles and temperature
Mass, color, temperature and pressure
Number of particles, density, volume and viscosity

items.explain: Gases are described by pressure, volume, number of particles (counted in moles) and temperature.

items.prompt: A gas is found to hold permanently charged ions. What is such a gas called?

options.label: A Bose gas
A noble gas
A diatomic gas
A plasma

items.explain: Gases that contain permanently charged ions are known as plasmas.

items.prompt: Why do gas particles generally attract each other more weakly than particles in a liquid or solid?

options.label: They are much lighter than liquid particles
They are widely separated from one another
They carry no charged regions at all
They move too slowly to interact

items.explain: Gas particles are widely separated and so have weaker intermolecular bonds than liquids or solids.

beats.title: Squeezing the invisible
beats.hook: A gas fills whatever holds it, yet it can still be squeezed into less room.

beats.prompt: You release gas at one end of an empty closed box. Where do its particles end up?
beats.explain: Gas particles spread apart to distribute themselves evenly throughout any container.

choices.label: Clustered near where they were released
choices.feedback: Gas particles spread apart rather than staying bunched up.

choices.label: Packed along the bottom
choices.feedback: That is how a liquid or solid might sit; gas particles distribute themselves throughout the container.

beats.prompt: When measuring a gas, sort each quantity by what it describes.
beats.explain: Measured characteristics are either in terms of the particles (velocity, pressure, temperature) or their surroundings (volume).

beats.prompt: One step in this account of Boyle's experiment is wrong. Which?

steps.text: Boyle trapped a gas in the closed end of a J-shaped tube.
The number of particles and the temperature stayed constant.
He added mercury, and the pressure on the gas rose, so its volume grew.
The pressure and volume of a gas therefore have an inverse relationship.

beats.explain: When the pressure was increased, the trapped gas's volume decreased, which is what makes the relationship inverse.

beats.prompt: You compare a 1-liter container of gas with a 1-liter container of liquid. Which holds fewer particles?
beats.explain: Gas particles are vastly separated and gases have low density compared with other states of matter.

choices.label: The liquid, since its particles are far apart
choices.feedback: It is the gas whose particles are vastly separated.

choices.label: The gas, since its particles are far apart
Both hold exactly the same number
choices.feedback: Gases have low density compared with other states, so equal volumes do not hold equal numbers.

paragraphs.heading: What a gas is
paragraphs.text: A gas is a state of matter with no fixed volume and no fixed shape. Like a liquid it is a fluid, but unlike a liquid it can be compressed. A pure gas is made of single atoms, as in the noble gas neon, or of molecules, as in oxygen (O₂) or carbon dioxide. Pure gases can also be mixed together, as they are in air.

paragraphs.heading: Particles far apart
paragraphs.text: What sets gases apart from liquids and solids is the huge distance between their particles. That spacing can even make some gases invisible to us. With the particles so widely spread, the forces between them are weaker than in liquids or solids. Gases also have low density and low viscosity compared with the other states, and their particles spread out until they are evenly distributed through any container.

paragraphs.heading: Forces between particles
paragraphs.text: The forces that remain come from electric attraction and repulsion. Parts of neighbouring particles with the same charge push apart, while opposite charges pull together. Molecules with polar bonds carry lasting charge imbalances, so they feel fairly strong forces, even though each molecule stays neutral overall. Non-polar molecules have only brief, random charges, and the forces these cause are called Van der Waals forces. A gas that holds permanently charged ions is called a plasma.

paragraphs.heading: Where gases sit
paragraphs.text: On the temperature scale, the gas state lies between liquid and plasma, and plasma marks its upper limit. At the very cold end lie degenerate quantum gases, which are drawing more and more attention. Dense atomic gases chilled to very low temperatures are sorted by their statistical behaviour into Bose gases and Fermi gases.

paragraphs.heading: Describing a gas
paragraphs.text: Since most gases are hard to observe directly, scientists describe them with four properties: pressure, volume, number of particles, which chemists count in moles, and temperature. Scientists including Robert Boyle, Jacques Charles, John Dalton, Amedeo Avogadro and Joseph Gay-Lussac studied these for many gases, and their work led to a formula linking them, the ideal gas law. Boyle, for instance, used a J-shaped tube and trapped gas in its closed end behind a column of mercury, which kept the amount and temperature of the gas fixed. As he added mercury and raised the pressure, the trapped gas shrank in volume.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word came from
paragraphs.text: The word gas was first used in the early 17th century by Jan Baptist van Helmont, a chemist from Brabant. He identified carbon dioxide, the first gas known other than air. His word seems to be a spelling of the Ancient Greek word chaos as it sounds in Dutch. In using it he followed an alchemical habit that goes back to Paracelsus, for whom chaos meant something like ultra-rarefied water.
